newsitem.title: UK: Sterling slides as Major sets election date.
newsitem.headline: Sterling slides as Major sets election date.

text.p: Sterling was weak though above six-week lows against the mark after British Prime Minister John Major announced the date of the general election, ending weeks of speculation.

Sterling recovered some ground after Major called the election for May 1 -- a date widely anticipated by relieved financial markets -- but later sank again to test fresh six-week lows of 2.6795 marks.
"There wasn't any surprise at all in the announcement. (Political) uncertainties are now out of the way and it looks like a relief for markets," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Sterling recovered slightly to 2.6855/65 marks after the official announcement from 2.6840 marks ahead of it.
But at 1348 GMT the pound stood at 2.6838/48 marks and floundering just off fresh six-week lows of 2.6795 marks.
Earlier on Monday sterling plunged two and a half pfennings to 2.6838 marks as speculation mounted that Major would make the long-awaited announcement on the election.
A powering mark in Europe, which rallied above 1,000 lire for the first time in two-weeks, also weighed on sterling.
"We are seeing a resurgent mark on the crosses," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns.
Against the dollar, sterling stood at $1.5915/25 at 1353 GMT and above lows of $1.5890, though still down from $1.6012 in late Europe on Friday.

Although the announcement of a May 1 election date came as no surprise, the fact that Major has opted for a relatively long election campaign could be a negative for sterling in some ways, said analysts.

"From the foreign investors' perspective, the longer it (the election campaign), the less favourable a light it will cast on the UK scene, if you've got two parties trading insults for six weeks," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International, said there are two aspects the market would focus on during the election campaign.
These, he said, would be how the campaign actually affects the polls and whether any signs of a shift in Labour's thinking emerge.
The latest NOP opinion poll published on Sunday showed Britain's opposition Labour Party has extended its lead over the Conservatives by seven points.
The NOP poll for the Sunday Times newspaper put Labour on 52 percent, a three point increase over last month, and the Conservatives down four on 27 percent.
Markets have widely discounted a Labour victory.

"If anything, (a Labour victory) could be a mild positive for sterling. Labour looks to be willing to keep tight fiscal and monetary policy in the near-term, and maybe more accommodative to (European) monetary union," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.

Some economists, however, have said Labour landslide could jolt sterling markets as it could give the party, out of government since 1979, a mandate to be tougher on economic policy. And some have even raised the possibility of the party reneging on some of its pre-election commitments.
